claims.text: Core-shell formation in high-entropy-alloy nanoparticles can overcome structural or chemical instability during operation at 773–1173 K.
The target initial material consists of crystalline, near-equiatomic solid-solution nanoparticles containing at least five metals.
A core-shell architecture can be formed in high-entropy-alloy nanoparticles.
The cited Al-Co-Cr-Fe-Ni material contains nanoparticles with a core-shell structure.
The proposed core-shell intervention is applicable throughout the 773–1173 K catalytic regime.
A core-shell structure enhances the thermal stability of high-entropy-alloy nanoparticles.
A core-shell structure prevents nanoparticle growth during high-temperature operation.
A core-shell structure prevents nanoparticle agglomeration during high-temperature operation.
Preventing growth and agglomeration preserves nanoparticle structural stability.
Preventing growth and agglomeration preserves nanoparticle chemical stability.
Core-shell high-entropy-alloy nanoparticles will exhibit better catalytic performance than otherwise identical nanoparticles without a core-shell structure.
Core-shell high-entropy-alloy nanoparticles will exhibit better operational stability than otherwise identical nanoparticles without a core-shell structure.
The hypothesis is intended to apply to exposure for several hours and to compositions containing at least five metals.
The mechanism by which core-shell formation affects structural and chemical stability is not fully understood.
A controlled thermal-exposure experiment will compare nanoparticles with and without a core-shell structure at 773–1173 K for several hours.
The hypothesis will be considered falsified if the core-shell samples show no improvement in both catalytic performance and stability relative to the non-core-shell controls.
